claim: Cognitive processes are mediated by computations in neural circuits and are often associated with gamma frequency oscillations in circuit activity.
source: Cognitive processes are mediated by computations in neural circuits and are often associated with gamma frequency oscillations in circuit activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between cognitive processes, neural computations, and gamma oscillations, representing established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Gamma activity and cognitive performance often co-vary within tasks and between individuals.
source: Gamma activity and cognitive performance often co-vary within tasks and between individuals, while cognitive deficits in psychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia are linked to altered gamma frequency network dynamics (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2012; Spellman and Gordon, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Uhlhaas and Singer, 2012 and Spellman and Gordon, 2014.

claim: Cognitive deficits in psychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia are linked to altered gamma frequency network dynamics.
source: Gamma activity and cognitive performance often co-vary within tasks and between individuals, while cognitive deficits in psychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia are linked to altered gamma frequency network dynamics (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2012; Spellman and Gordon, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Uhlhaas and Singer, 2012 and Spellman and Gordon, 2014.

claim: Psychiatric disorders are linked to changes in the efficacy of excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic synapses.
source: Such disorders are also linked to changes in the efficacy of excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic synapses (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Lewis et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003 and Lewis et al., 2012.

claim: Rate coded computations and gamma oscillations arise from shared circuit mechanisms.
source: Evidence that rate coded computations and gamma oscillations arise from shared circuit mechanisms could be interpreted to support this view (Lundqvist et al., 2010; Pastoll et al., 2013), which predicts that when synaptic properties of a circuit are altered then gamma activity and the output of the rate-coded computation will co-vary.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lundqvist et al., 2010 and Pastoll et al., 2013.

claim: The rate-coded firing of grid cells in the MEC is a well-studied feature of neural circuits for spatial cognition.
source: The rate-coded firing of grid cells in the MEC is a well-studied feature of neural circuits for spatial cognition (Moser and Moser, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moser and Moser, 2013.

claim: During exploration of an environment individual grid cells are active at multiple locations that together follow a hexagonal grid-like organization.
source: During exploration of an environment individual grid cells are active at multiple locations that together follow a hexagonal grid-like organization.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of grid cells based on experimental observations.

claim: MEC circuits generate periods of activity in the high gamma frequency range (60–120 Hz) nested within a slower theta (8–12 Hz) frequency network oscillation.
source: At the same time MEC circuits generate periods of activity in the high gamma frequency range (60–120 Hz) nested within a slower theta (8–12 Hz) frequency network oscillation (Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1998.

claim: Analysis of spatial correlations in grid firing, of manipulations to grid circuits, and recording of grid cell membrane potential in behaving animals, collectively point towards continuous two-dimensional network attractor states as explanations for grid firing.
source: Analysis of spatial correlations in grid firing, of manipulations to grid circuits, and recording of grid cell membrane potential in behaving animals, collectively point towards continuous two-dimensional network attractor states as explanations for grid firing (Bonnevie et al., 2013; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonnevie et al., 2013; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Yoon et al., 2013.

claim: In layer II of the MEC, stellate cells that project to the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus are the major population of excitatory neurons.
source: In layer II of the MEC, which has the highest known density of grid cells (Sargolini et al., 2006), stellate cells that project to the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus are the major population of excitatory neurons (Gatome et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sargolini et al., 2006 and Gatome et al., 2010.

claim: Excitatory neurons in layer II of the MEC do not appear to influence one another directly but instead interact via intermediate inhibitory neurons.
source: These excitatory (E) neurons do not appear to influence one another directly but instead interact via intermediate inhibitory (I) neurons (Dhillon and Jones, 2000; Couey et al., 2013; Pastoll et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dhillon and Jones, 2000; Couey et al., 2013; Pastoll et al., 2013.

claim: Models that explicitly incorporate recurrent E-I-E connectivity can account for grid firing through velocity-dependent update of network attractor states.
source: Models that explicitly incorporate this recurrent E-I-E connectivity can account for grid firing through velocity-dependent update of network attractor states (Pastoll et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pastoll et al., 2013.

claim: When E-I-E models are implemented with excitable spiking neurons they also account for theta-nested gamma frequency network oscillations.
source: When these models are implemented with excitable spiking neurons they also account for theta-nested gamma frequency network oscillations (Pastoll et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pastoll et al., 2013.

claim: Moderate intrinsic noise massively increases the range of synaptic strengths supporting gamma oscillations and grid computation.
source: We show that moderate intrinsic noise massively increases the range of synaptic strengths supporting gamma oscillations and grid computation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: With moderate noise, variation in excitatory or inhibitory synaptic strength tunes the amplitude and frequency of gamma activity without disrupting grid firing.
source: With moderate noise, variation in excitatory or inhibitory synaptic strength tunes the amplitude and frequency of gamma activity without disrupting grid firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The beneficial role for noise results from disruption of epileptic-like network states.
source: This beneficial role for noise results from disruption of epileptic-like network states.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Moderate noise promotes independent control of multiplexed firing rate- and gamma-based computational mechanisms.
source: Thus, moderate noise promotes independent control of multiplexed firing rate- and gamma-based computational mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: In the absence of noise grid firing is supported in relatively restricted regions of parameter space.
source: In the absence of noise grid firing is supported in relatively restricted regions of parameter space.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Optimal levels of noise promote grid firing by reducing the sensitivity of grid computations to the strength of recurrent synaptic connections, particularly when inhibition is relatively strong and excitation is weak.
source: Optimal levels of noise, which produce single cell membrane potential fluctuations of a similar amplitude to experimental observations (Domnisoru et al., 2013; Pastoll et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013), promote grid firing by reducing the sensitivity of grid computations to the strength of recurrent synaptic connections, particularly when inhibition is relatively strong and excitation is weak.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citations to experimental observations.

claim: In networks that generate grid firing fields in the presence of moderate noise, I cell firing fields have a much lower spatial information content and spatial sparsity than the corresponding E cell firing fields.
source: However, in networks that we evaluate here in which E cells have grid firing fields in the presence of moderate noise, I cell firing fields also have a much lower spatial information content and spatial sparsity than the corresponding E cell firing fields (E cells: spatial sparsity 0.788 ± 0.061, spatial information: 1.749 ± 0.32 bits/spike; I cells: spatial sparsity 0.239 ± 0.018, spatial information 0.243 ± 0.024 bits/spike; p < 10−16 for comparisons of both spatial sparsity and information; paired t-test; data range is indicated as mean ± standard deviation) (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from simulations.

claim: Spatial autocorrelograms of simulated I cell firing fields do not contain the six hexagonally organized peaks that are characteristic of grid fields.
source: Spatial autocorrelograms of simulated I cell firing fields also do not contain the six hexagonally organized peaks that are characteristic of grid fields (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of autocorrelograms in Figure 2A-C.

claim: I cell spatial autocorrelograms produce positive grid scores (0.39 ± 0.16).
source: Nevertheless, I cell spatial autocorrelograms produce positive grid scores (0.39 ± 0.16; Figure 2—figure supplement 3), although these are reduced compared to scores for the E cells in the same networks (E cells: 0.796 ± 0.157; p < 10−16; paired t-test; mean ± SD) and in many networks are below the threshold considered previously to qualify as grid like (cf. Figure 4B of Buetfering et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from simulations.

claim: The dependence of I cell spatial firing on gE, gI and noise appears to be similar to that of E cells.
source: When we evaluated the dependence of I cell spatial firing on gE, gI and noise, it appeared to be similar to that of E cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In E-I networks with uncorrelated spatial input to each I cell, E cells had grid scores of 0.57 ± 0.25, spatial sparsity of 0.78 ± 0.03 and spatial information of 1.69 ± 0.18 bits/spike.
source: In these simulations E cells had grid scores of 0.57 ± 0.25, spatial sparsity of 0.78 ± 0.03 and spatial information of 1.69 ± 0.18 bits/spike, whereas I cells had grid scores of 0.16 ± 0.2 (p < 10−16, paired t-test), spatial sparsity of 0.21 ± 0.01 (p < 10−16, paired t-test) and spatial information of 0.2 ± 0.01 bits/spike (p < 10−16, paired t-test; range of all data sets is mean ± SD).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from simulations with uncorrelated spatial input to I cells.

claim: In E-I networks with uncorrelated spatial input to each I cell, I cells had grid scores of 0.16 ± 0.2, spatial sparsity of 0.21 ± 0.01 and spatial information of 0.2 ± 0.01 bits/spike.
source: In these simulations E cells had grid scores of 0.57 ± 0.25, spatial sparsity of 0.78 ± 0.03 and spatial information of 1.69 ± 0.18 bits/spike, whereas I cells had grid scores of 0.16 ± 0.2 (p < 10−16, paired t-test), spatial sparsity of 0.21 ± 0.01 (p < 10−16, paired t-test) and spatial information of 0.2 ± 0.01 bits/spike (p < 10−16, paired t-test; range of all data sets is mean ± SD).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from simulations with uncorrelated spatial input to I cells.

claim: Grid firing by E cells in E-I networks is relatively robust to disruption of the rotational symmetry of I cell firing fields.
source: Thus, spatial firing of I cells has a similar dependence on noise, gE and gI to grid cells, conventional indices of spatial firing are nevertheless much lower for I cells in E-I networks compared to E cells, and grid firing by E cells in E-I networks is relatively robust to disruption of the rotational symmetry of I cell firing fields.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations with uncorrelated spatial input to I cells.

claim: Attractor circuit computations that generate grid firing fields require specific tuning of gE and gI.
source: Together these simulations demonstrate that attractor circuit computations that generate grid firing fields require specific tuning of gE and gI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the absence of noise, gamma frequency activity only occurred for a narrow range of gI and gE.
source: In the absence of noise gamma frequency activity only occurred for a narrow range of gI and gE (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Following addition of moderate noise the region of parameter space that supports gamma activity was massively expanded.
source: Strikingly, following addition of moderate noise the region of parameter space that supports gamma activity was massively expanded (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Within the parameter space supporting gamma activity, the amplitude of gamma increased with increasing inhibition, whereas the frequency was reduced.
source: Within this space, the amplitude of gamma increased with increasing inhibition, whereas the frequency was reduced.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: As noise is increased further the amplitude and frequency of gamma oscillations are reduced.
source: As noise is increased further the amplitude and frequency of gamma oscillations are reduced (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There is no strong linear relationship between gamma amplitude or gamma frequency and grid score.
source: However, we did not find any evidence for strong linear relationships between gamma amplitude or gamma frequency and grid score (R2 < 0.12 for all comparisons), while gamma amplitude and frequency provided only modest amounts of information about grid scores (0.27 < MIC < 0.33 and 0.27 < MIC < 0.37 respectively).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the relationship between gamma and grid scores.

claim: Neither the frequency nor the power of gamma appears to be a good predictor of grid firing.
source: Thus, neither the frequency nor the power of gamma appears to be a good predictor of grid firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the relationship between gamma and grid scores.

claim: Circuits generating robust grid fields (grid score >0.5) can generate almost the complete observed range of gamma amplitudes (0.02 < autocorrelation peak < 0.59) and frequencies (31 Hz < frequency < 102 Hz).
source: When we considered only regions of parameter space that generate robust grid fields (grid score >0.5), we found circuits generating almost the complete observed range of gamma amplitudes (0.02 < autocorrelation peak < 0.59) and frequencies (31 Hz < frequency < 102 Hz) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Variation of synaptic strength across the region of E-I space that supports grid firing can be used to tune the properties of gamma activity while maintaining the ability of the network to generate grid fields.
source: Thus, variation of synaptic strength across this region of E-I space can be used to tune the properties of gamma activity while maintaining the ability of the network to generate grid fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: For deterministic simulation of points in parameter space that are able to generate grid patterns, a single stable bump of activity emerged over the first 2.5 s of simulated time.
source: For deterministic simulation of the points in parameter space considered in Figure 2Aa, which are able to generate grid patterns, we found that a single stable bump of activity emerged over the first 2.5 s of simulated time (Figure 4Aa).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4Aa.

claim: For deterministic simulation of points in parameter space that did not generate grid patterns, a single stable bump fails to emerge.
source: In contrast, for deterministic simulation of the point considered in 2Ab, which in deterministic simulations did not generate grid patterns, a single stable bump fails to emerge (Figure 4Ab).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4Ab.

claim: When gI is low there is a high probability of bump formation as well as grid firing, whereas when gI is high the probability of both is reduced in deterministic networks.
source: Quantification across the wider space of gE and gI values (see 'Materials and methods') indicated that when gI is low there is a high probability of bump formation as well as grid firing, whereas when gI is high the probability of both is reduced (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For circuits with intrinsically noisy neurons activity bumps emerged in the first 1.25 s following initialization of the network.
source: In contrast to the deterministic condition, for circuits with intrinsically noisy neurons activity bumps emerged in the first 1.25 s following initialization of the network (Figure 4Ac–e) and the area of parameter space that supported bump formation was much larger than that supporting grid firing (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4Ac-e and Figure 4B.

claim: Bump formation is necessary, although not sufficient for grid formation.
source: Plotting gridness scores as a function of bump probability indicated that bump formation was necessary, although not sufficient for grid formation (Figure 4C), while plotting the first autocorrelation peak as a function of bump probability supported our conclusion that grid computation and gamma activity are not closely related (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Noise promotes formation of attractor bumps in network activity and in deterministic simulations the failure of the circuit to generate attractor states largely accounts for disrupted grid firing.
source: Together, these data indicate that noise promotes formation of attractor bumps in network activity and in deterministic simulations the failure of the circuit to generate attractor states largely accounts for disrupted grid firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In noisy networks the presence of low grid scores for networks with high bump scores is explained by sensitivity of these network configurations to noise-induced drift.
source: In noisy networks the presence of low grid scores for networks with high bump scores (Figure 4C) is explained by sensitivity of these network configurations to noise-induced drift.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4Ac-e.

claim: Intrinsic noise has two opposing effects on bump formation: moderate noise promotes emergence of bumps and grids, while across all of parameter space noise reduces bump stability leading to deterioration of grids.
source: Thus, intrinsic noise has two opposing effects on bump formation. For much of the parameter space we consider moderate noise promotes emergence of bumps and grids, while across all of parameter space noise reduces bump stability leading to deterioration of grids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of noise the network generates hyper-synchronous seizure-like states at the start of each theta cycle.
source: When we examined times of action potentials generated by all neurons in this circuit, we find that in the absence of noise the network generates hyper-synchronous seizure-like states at the start of each theta cycle (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When moderate noise is added to the circuit only a subset of E-cells are active on each theta cycle, forming an activity bump.
source: When moderate noise is added to the circuit only a subset of E-cells are active on each theta cycle, forming an activity bump (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: With increased noise there is a similar overall pattern of activity, but spike timing becomes more variable, causing the bumps to drift and reducing the degree of synchronization at gamma frequencies.
source: With increased noise there is a similar overall pattern of activity, but spike timing becomes more variable, causing the bumps to drift and reducing the degree of synchronization at gamma frequencies (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the absence of noise epochs with highly synchronized activity were found for almost all combinations of gE and gI, whereas these seizure-like events were absent in simulations where noise was present.
source: Strikingly, we found that in the absence of noise epochs with highly synchronized activity were found for almost all combinations of gE and gI, whereas these seizure-like events were absent in simulations where noise was present (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For values of gE and gI where grid fields are present, the proportion of theta cycles having events with population-average rate >300 Hz was relatively low, indicating that seizure-like events are rare.
source: For values of gE and gI where grid fields are present PE-rate > 300 was relatively low, indicating that seizure-like events are indeed rare (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: While grid firing is compatible with occasional seizure-like events, when seizure-like events occur on the majority of theta cycles then grid firing is prevented.
source: Thus, while grid firing is compatible with occasional seizure-like events, when seizure-like events occur on the majority of theta cycles then grid firing is prevented.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Moderate noise prevents emergence of seizure like states by disrupting synchronization of the attractor network by the shared theta frequency drive.
source: Together, these data indicate that moderate noise prevents emergence of seizure like states by disrupting synchronization of the attractor network by the shared theta frequency drive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In networks with moderate noise theta drive promotes grid firing and enables a wide range of gamma frequencies to be generated without disrupting grid firing.
source: In networks with moderate noise theta drive promotes grid firing and enables a wide range of gamma frequencies to be generated without disrupting grid firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: In E-I-I networks, in the absence of noise, grid firing emerges across a much larger region of parameter space compared to E-I networks.
source: In the resulting E-I-I networks, in the absence of noise, grid firing emerges across a much larger region of parameter space compared to E-I networks (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4.

claim: In E-I-I networks, as in E-I networks occasional seizure like activity was present across a wide range of gE and gI, and gamma frequency activity was largely absent in the absence of noise.
source: However, as in E-I networks occasional seizure like activity was present across a wide range of gE and gI (Figure 7—figure supplement 5), and gamma frequency activity was largely absent (Figure 7D,G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D, G and Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Following addition of noise with standard deviation of 150 pA to E-I-I networks, grid firing was maintained, seizure like activity was abolished, and gamma like activity emerged.
source: Following addition of noise with standard deviation of 150 pA to E-I-I networks, grid firing was maintained, seizure like activity was abolished, and gamma like activity emerged (Figure 7B,E,H and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B, E, H and Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Gamma activity had a higher frequency in E-I-I compared to E-I networks, with a greater proportion of the parameter space supporting gamma frequencies >80 Hz.
source: Gamma activity had a higher frequency in E-I-I compared to E-I networks, with a greater proportion of the parameter space supporting gamma frequencies >80 Hz.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of gamma frequency data in E-I and E-I-I networks.

claim: E-I-I networks maintain the ability, in the presence of moderate noise, for variation in gE and gI to tune gamma oscillations without interfering with grid firing.
source: Nevertheless, E-I-I networks maintain the ability, in the presence of moderate noise, for variation in gE and gI to tune gamma oscillations without interfering with grid firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: While gamma oscillations and grid firing are both sensitive to the strength of excitatory and inhibitory connections, their relationship differs.
source: We find that while gamma oscillations and grid firing are both sensitive to the strength of excitatory and inhibitory connections, their relationship differs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Gamma activity provides little information about grid firing or the presence of underlying network attractor states.
source: Although their underlying synaptic substrates are identical, gamma activity nevertheless provides little information about grid firing or the presence of underlying network attractor states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Gamma activity is not a good predictor of rate-coded computation.
source: Thus, gamma activity is not a good predictor of rate-coded computation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: The range of E- and I- synaptic strengths that support gamma and grid firing is massively increased by moderate intrinsic noise through a mechanism involving suppression of seizure-like events.
source: Unexpectedly, we find the range of E- and I- synaptic strengths that support gamma and grid firing is massively increased by moderate intrinsic noise through a mechanism involving suppression of seizure-like events.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: In the presence of moderate noise differences in synaptic strength can tune the amplitude and frequency of gamma across a wide range with little effect on grid firing.
source: In the presence of moderate noise differences in synaptic strength can tune the amplitude and frequency of gamma across a wide range with little effect on grid firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The model comprises a network of exponential integrate and fire neurons implemented as a custom-made module of the NEST simulator.
source: The model comprised a network of exponential integrate and fire neurons (Fourcaud-Trocmé et al., 2003) implemented as a custom-made module of the NEST simulator (Gewaltig and Diesmann, 2007).
evidence: This describes the computational implementation of the model.

claim: The network consists of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations of neurons that were arranged on a twisted torus with dimensions of 34 × 30 neurons.
source: The network investigated in the majority of simulations (Figures 1–6) is modified from that in Pastoll et al. (2013) and consists of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations of neurons that were arranged on a twisted torus with dimensions of 34 × 30 neurons.
evidence: This describes the structure of the network model.
